title: Your Verilog to Tiny Tapeout
subtitle: A short practical guide using an existing eight-bit shift register

pages.title: Your Verilog → a checked chip layout
pages.intro: You already have a working Verilog design. This guide shows how to put it inside Tiny Tapeout, test the connections and build its layout. In the local research checkout, src, test and info.yaml are directly at the project root. We use an eight-bit shift register throughout.
actions: Keep this guide beside your browser. Use the interactive HTML version for the clock experiment and tick each checkpoint as you finish.

Sign in to a free GitHub account. Download shift-register-starter.zip and extract it: on Windows, right-click → Extract All. Open the extracted folder containing info.yaml, src, test and docs. GitHub stores your project and runs the tools.
Follow pages 2–14 in order. Pages 13–14 cover gate-level simulation (GLS); page 15 is your final checklist and help sheet. You need no chip board or local tool installation for this browser route.
pages.checkpoint: I have opened the guide, signed in to GitHub and found the starter ZIP.

terms.meaning: A service that combines small circuit designs on a shared chip. Its template includes the build tools.
The shapes and wires used to manufacture the circuit. GDS is the file format that stores them.

links.label: Open GitHub / create a free account

pages.title: 1. Start with the design you already have
pages.intro: Our starting file is shift_register.v. It stores eight bits. Each rising clock edge moves the bits one position towards bit 7 and puts serial_in into bit 0, when enable is 1.
actions: In the extracted folder, open src/shift_register.v with a text editor such as Notepad or VS Code. This is the reusable circuit; it does not contain Tiny Tapeout pin names.
Read its rule: reset wins; otherwise enable shifts; otherwise the stored value stays the same. Reset is synchronous: it takes effect at a rising clock edge.
Try the clock experiment in the HTML guide. From reset, shift in 1, then 0, then 1. Predict the eight-bit output after each edge.

predict.question: Starting at 00000000, what do inputs 1, 0, 1 produce after three enabled edges?

pages.checkpoint: I know my circuit’s reset polarity, shift direction and enable behaviour.

terms.meaning: The Verilog description of the circuit’s behaviour and registers.

pages.title: 2. Make your own Tiny Tapeout project
pages.intro: A template is a ready-made set of folders and automation. A repository is your own saved project on GitHub.
actions: Open the official HDL templates page below. Choose the SKY Verilog template used in this lesson. Confirm the repository is TinyTapeout/ttsky-verilog-template.
Sign in. Select Use this template → Create a new repository. Choose your own account as Owner.
Name it tt-shift-register, choose Public, and create it. Check that the new page begins with YOUR username. All later edits happen in this new repository.

image.caption: GitHub’s official screenshot shows the template menu. Use this control on the SKY template page.

pages.checkpoint: My repository belongs to my account and contains src, test, docs and info.yaml.

pages.title: 3. Turn on the build and results page
pages.intro: GitHub Actions runs the checks for you. GitHub Pages displays the finished layout in a browser.
actions: In your new repository, open Actions. If you see an enable-workflows banner, enable it; otherwise continue.
Open Settings → Pages. Under Build and deployment, change Source to GitHub Actions.
Return to Code. Keep the template’s .github folder, src/config.json and test/requirements.txt. The starter changes your design files, while these files supply the tools.

image.caption: 1 Settings → 2 Pages → 3 GitHub Actions. Official FAQ screenshot; step 2 annotation added.

pages.checkpoint: Actions is available and Pages → Source says GitHub Actions.

terms.meaning: A saved recipe of jobs that GitHub runs, such as test or gds.

pages.title: 4. Plan how your signals reach the chip pins
pages.intro: Your circuit has its own signal names. Tiny Tapeout expects a fixed set of ports. A wrapper is a small Verilog module that connects the two.
actions: Use ui_in[0] for serial_in and ui_in[1] for the circuit’s enable. Bits 2–7 are unused.
Connect clk directly. The platform’s rst_n is active low: 0 requests reset. Our circuit’s rst is active high, so connect rst to ~rst_n.
Send all eight q bits to uo_out. We do not use the bidirectional pins: set uio_out and uio_oe to zero. Keep all required wrapper ports.

predict.question: Is ena the same signal as our shift enable?
predict.answer: No. ena selects this project on the shared chip. Our shift enable is ui_in[1]. This core uses only ui_in[1] to decide whether to shift.

pages.checkpoint: I can trace every used chip pin to a signal in my existing design.

terms.meaning: A named input or output of a Verilog module.
The function is requested with 0 rather than 1.

pages.title: 5. Add the wrapper around your design
pages.intro: Open the supplied project.v. It creates one instance of your shift register and connects the signals from page 5. The shift-register code itself stays reusable.
actions: Use the complete supplied project.v as the replacement for the template’s example.
For this first run, keep tt_um_student_shift_register unchanged everywhere. For a later submission, choose your own unique name beginning tt_um_ and change all three locations on page 7.
Notice that ~ means invert: ~rst_n converts the reset convention. uio_oe = 0 makes every bidirectional pin an input.
pages.checkpoint: My wrapper has the eight required ports and instantiates shift_register with the intended connections.

pages.title: 6. Tell both tools which files to use
pages.intro: The layout builder and simulator read separate source lists. Both must find your core and wrapper. The top module is the outermost circuit the tools should build.
actions: In info.yaml, under project, use top_module: "tt_um_student_shift_register" and source_files: ["project.v", "shift_register.v"]. These filenames refer to files inside src.
In test/Makefile, set PROJECT_SOURCES = project.v shift_register.v. Use the supplied complete Makefile so the surrounding test setup remains intact.
In test/tb.v, the module instantiated as user_project must be tt_um_student_shift_register. The supplied tb.v already does this.
pages.checkpoint: All three top-module names match; both source lists contain both Verilog files.

terms.meaning: Simulation-only code that connects the design to its test. It is not manufactured.

pages.title: 7. Describe the design and its clock
pages.intro: The metadata identifies your project. The datasheet explains how someone can use its pins.
actions: Open the supplied info.yaml. Replace the example author with your name. Keep meaningful title and description text, language Verilog, and the pin labels that match page 5. Keep every required pin key.
Open docs/info.md. Check its How it works, How to test and External hardware sections. It should say: reset clears on an edge; ui_in[1] enables shifting; ui_in[0] supplies the next bit.

For the first exercise keep the supplied 50 MHz target and the current SKY configuration’s 20 ns clock period. The Python test uses 20 ns too. Metadata alone does not change the physical timing constraint.

rows: 10 ns low + 5 ns to sample + 5 ns = 20 ns

pages.checkpoint: My descriptions, pin map and clock settings agree with the actual design.

terms.meaning: Settings and descriptions about your project.
50 million clock cycles each second; one cycle lasts 20 nanoseconds.

pages.title: 8. Replace the example test with your test
pages.intro: The template’s adder test cannot verify a shift register. Our Python test drives the wrapper’s pins and checks the output after clock edges.
actions: In the extracted folder, open test/test.py. Use this complete file to replace the template’s test/test.py. cocotb is the Python tool that talks to the Verilog simulator.
Read the phases: reset, shift known bits, hold, shift more than eight bits so old data leaves, and reset while enable is 1. It also checks that unused outputs and bidirectional directions stay zero.
For your own design, change the expected result rule and input sequence to match its written behaviour. Keep checks at the external ports so the same test can run on the gate-level circuit.

code.text:
# Shift the previous value and add the new bit.
expected = ((expected << 1) | bit) & 0xFF
assert await cycle(bit) == expected

predict.question: After shifting 1 eight times from reset, what should the output be? What if enable then becomes 0?
predict.answer: 11111111. With enable = 0 it stays 11111111, even when serial_in changes.

pages.checkpoint: My test checks my circuit’s behaviour rather than the template’s example.

terms.meaning: Running a model of the circuit before making hardware.
A check that stops the test when the observed result differs from the expected one.

pages.title: 9. Upload the complete seven-file adaptation
pages.intro: Extract shift-register-starter.zip. Open its contents until you see info.yaml beside src, test and docs.
actions: In your own repository’s root, select Add file → Upload files. Drag info.yaml and the src, test and docs folders from INSIDE the extracted starter folder.
Check the paths: src/shift_register.v, src/project.v, test/Makefile, test/tb.v, test/test.py, docs/info.md and info.yaml. There must be no extra starter-folder prefix.

Enter Add shift register. For this personal practice repository choose Commit directly to main and save. A commit is a saved version. If GitHub requires a new branch, create a pull request and merge it into main. Check all seven files on main and note its commit identifier.

image.caption: GitHub’s official Add file screenshot locates the upload control. Upload into your repository root.

pages.checkpoint: All seven files are saved at the intended paths, and the template infrastructure is still present.

help.fix: Open each existing file, select the pencil, replace its contents and commit. For src/shift_register.v use Add file → Create new file inside src. Check workflows only after all seven files are saved.

pages.title: 10. Check that your shift register passes
pages.intro: Each saved version can start checks. Open the run for the commit that contains your complete adaptation.
actions: Select Actions → test → the run for your final commit. Confirm its branch and commit identifier.
Open the test job and expand Run tests. Read the final test summary: there must be no failures or errors. A green run from before your edit proves nothing about your new design.
If it fails, open the first assertion or compilation error. Fix that cause and save a new commit. The help sheet on page 15 covers common causes.

image.caption: Official TEMPLATE Actions screen, for navigation only. Its red crosses are failed template runs, not your result. Your shift-register run has its own commit and result.

predict.question: What does a passing test establish?
predict.answer: The adapted circuit passed the cases and assertions you wrote. It does not prove every possible behaviour, timing corner or manufactured chip.

pages.checkpoint: The RTL test passed for my exact final commit, with zero failures and errors.

terms.meaning: A simulation of your Verilog source before it is converted into physical gates.

pages.title: 11. Build, check and look at the layout
pages.intro: The gds workflow turns Verilog into physical gates and wires. The docs workflow builds your datasheet. These run separately from the RTL test.
actions: Open the docs workflow for the same commit. Confirm it succeeds. On its Summary page, scroll to Artifacts and download PDF; extract it and open datasheet.pdf. Check its pin table.
Open the gds workflow for that commit. Wait for the layout build, precheck, gate-level test and viewer jobs to complete successfully. Job labels can vary; open each job to see what ran.

Open the published Pages/viewer link from the run or repository Deployments. Zoom into the layout. On the gds run’s Summary page, scroll to Artifacts: download tt_submission (layout package) and GDS_logs (reports). Artifact names may change in later templates.

rows: Place gates and connect them; inspect timing and geometry reports
Check the design fits Tiny Tapeout’s integration rules
Run your test against the generated gate connections
Publish an image/browser view of the layout

pages.checkpoint: RTL, docs and every required gds job passed for one commit; I can open its layout and artifacts.

terms.meaning: A downloadable file produced by a workflow.
The circuit represented by the actual logic cells chosen during the build.

pages.title: 12. See what changes for gate-level simulation
pages.intro: Gate-Level Simulation (GLS) checks the circuit after the tools have converted your Verilog into logic cells. We run the same test at the same external pins.
actions: Keep test/test.py checking ui_in, rst_n and uo_out, as supplied. Internal names such as core.q can disappear when the circuit is built; the chip’s external ports remain the test interface.
Keep the GL_TEST sections in the supplied test/tb.v. Gate-level cells need power connections: VPWR is tied to 1 and VGND to 0 in the simulation fixture.

The gds workflow’s gl_test job downloads the generated netlist and matching SKY130 cell models. It selects the Makefile’s gate-level branch with GATES=yes. The cloud job supplies these dependencies; no local setup is needed.

rows: Logic cells connected by the build
GL_TEST fixture connects VPWR and VGND

pages.checkpoint: My test uses the wrapper ports, and the supplied fixture and gate-level Makefile branch are intact.

terms.meaning: A generated description of logic cells and the wires joining them.

pages.title: 13. Open the GLS job and check its evidence
pages.intro: The template starts GLS automatically after the GDS build succeeds. A successful RTL test and a successful GDS build do not replace this separate test.
actions: Open Actions → gds → the run for your complete commit. Select gl_test in Jobs. If it is waiting, let gds finish; if it was skipped, inspect the failed build first.

Expand GL test, then Run tests. Read the cocotb summary. Expect PASS with zero failed tests. For this supplied test, the summary should report TESTS=1, PASS=1, FAIL=0. The whole gl_test job must also finish successfully.

Return to the run’s Summary page. Under Artifacts, download gatelevel_test_results. Extract it and open results.xml with a text editor: check for test results with no failure or error entries. Keep the supplied tb.fst or tb.vcd waveform too.

image.caption: Genuine successful gl_test job from the earlier COUNTER example at commit 61ef06b. It shows where to open GL test; it is not a shift-register result.

help.fix: Read the first failed assertion. Check reset, the three top-module names and GL_TEST power connections. If necessary inspect the downloaded waveform at the failing time. Compare the same external pins and expected values used by the RTL test.

predict.question: Does this GLS result prove that every timing requirement is met?
predict.answer: No. This is a functional gate-level test. Inspect the build’s separate timing reports as well; this walkthrough does not run an SDF timing-annotated simulation.

pages.checkpoint: The gl_test job passed for the same commit; I saved its results XML and waveform.

links.label: Open the genuine counter GLS example

pages.title: 14. Keep your result and use the guide again
pages.intro: You have finished this exercise when your adapted circuit is tested and its checked layout is archived. Fabrication is a separate later step.
actions: Save the repository URL, commit identifier, test/gds/docs run links, downloaded GDS/reports and datasheet together. Match every item to the same commit.
Use the checklist: pin map agrees; three names agree; two source lists agree; RTL and GLS pass; docs pass; all required gds jobs pass; layout and evidence are saved.

For another existing Verilog design, reuse this route: describe its behaviour, map its pins, wrap it, list its sources and write its tests. For an approved fabrication submission, choose the matching shuttle and follow the submission app’s current checks.

help.fix: Page 7: check both source lists, filename case and the three top-module names.
Pages 5 and 9: check reset polarity, ui_in bit numbers, shift direction and expected values.
Page 8: complete title/author/description and the three datasheet sections; preserve YAML indentation and pin keys.
Page 4: set Pages Source to GitHub Actions. Follow the linked FAQ’s rerun procedure.

help.problem: Layout build or gate-level test fails
help.fix: Open the first failing job’s log. Read synthesis/timing/geometry warnings. Correct the cause; unchanged reruns will not repair the design.

pages.checkpoint: I have saved a checked layout package for one identifiable commit.
